items.followUp: Differentiate between a dilute solution and a concentrated solution.

rubric.why: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that dissolves at a particular temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a given temperature.

rubric.why: An unsaturated solution contains less than the maximum amount of dissolved solute and can dissolve more.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute than it currently contains.

modelAnswer: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a particular temperature.
An unsaturated solution contains less than this maximum amount and can dissolve more solute at that temperature.

items.followUp: Why does a colloidal solution show the Tyndall effect while a true solution does not?

rubric.why: True-solution particles are too small to scatter light visibly.
rubric.description: Explains why a true solution does not show the Tyndall effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the small size of true-solution particles with their inability to scatter light visibly.

rubric.why: Suspension particles settle on standing and do not produce the visible Tyndall cone characteristic of a colloid.
rubric.description: Explains why a suspension does not show the characteristic Tyndall effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that suspension particles settle and do not produce the characteristic visible Tyndall effect.

modelAnswer: In a true solution, the solute particles are too small to scatter light, so no visible Tyndall effect is observed.
Suspension particles are large and settle on standing, so they do not produce the visible Tyndall cone characteristic of a colloid.

items.followUp: Write the chemical formula of aluminium chloride using the criss-cross method.

rubric.why: The formula-writing method begins by identifying the symbols and valencies of the elements or ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the symbols and valencies of the elements or ions are written first.

rubric.why: The valencies are interchanged as subscripts and reduced to the simplest ratio where possible.
rubric.description: Applies the criss-cross method and simplifies if needed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for interchanging valencies as subscripts and simplifying the ratio if possible.

rubric.why: Magnesium chloride is a correct example with the formula MgCl₂.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for writing MgCl₂ as the formula for magnesium chloride.

rubric.why: Aluminium oxide is a correct example with the formula Al₂O₃.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for writing Al₂O₃ as the formula for aluminium oxide.

rubric.why: Calcium hydroxide is a correct example with the formula Ca(OH)₂.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for writing Ca(OH)₂ as the formula for calcium hydroxide.

modelAnswer: Write the symbols of the ions or elements and write their valencies above them.
Interchange the valencies and write them as subscripts; reduce them to the simplest whole-number ratio, if possible.
For magnesium chloride: Mg has valency 2 and Cl has valency 1; therefore, the formula is MgCl₂.
For aluminium oxide: Al has valency 3 and O has valency 2; therefore, the formula is Al₂O₃.
For calcium hydroxide: Ca has valency 2 and OH has valency 1; therefore, the formula is Ca(OH)₂.

items.followUp: Explain the formation of the hydronium ion as an example of a coordinate covalent bond.

rubric.why: A dative covalent bond has a shared pair of electrons, both of which are donated by one atom.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for identifying a shared pair of electrons and 1 for stating that both electrons are donated by one atom.

rubric.why: The donor supplies a lone pair, which is accepted by another atom or ion.
rubric.description: Explains the donor and acceptor roles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the donor as the atom that supplies a lone pair and the acceptor as the recipient.

rubric.why: Ammonia donates a lone pair to H⁺ to form NH₄⁺.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the ammonia-to-ammonium example, including the reactant species and product ion.

modelAnswer: A dative covalent bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are donated by one atom.
The atom donating the lone pair is the donor; the atom accepting it is the acceptor.
For example, in NH₃, nitrogen donates a lone pair to H⁺ to form NH₄⁺.
This bond may be represented by an arrow from the donor to the acceptor: H₃N→H⁺.

items.followUp: Give five differences between Rutherford’s atomic model and Bohr’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Rutherford allowed electrons to move in any orbit, while Bohr proposed only certain fixed orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for contrasting Rutherford’s any-orbit model with Bohr’s fixed orbits.

rubric.why: Bohr assigned a definite energy to each permitted orbit, unlike Rutherford’s model.
rubric.description: Compares the energy of the orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Bohr’s allowed orbits have definite energies, unlike Rutherford’s model.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability, whereas Bohr described stable orbits.
rubric.description: Compares the explanation of atomic stability.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for contrasting Rutherford’s failure to explain stability with Bohr’s stable orbits.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s model implied continuous radiation by revolving electrons; Bohr proposed that electrons do not radiate energy in permitted orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for contrasting continuous radiation in Rutherford’s model with no radiation in Bohr’s permitted orbits.

rubric.why: Bohr explained line spectra by electron transitions between energy levels; Rutherford’s model did not explain them.
rubric.description: Compares the explanation of atomic line spectra.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for connecting Bohr’s explanation of line spectra with electron transitions between energy levels.

modelAnswer: 1. Rutherford proposed that electrons revolve around the nucleus in any orbit; Bohr proposed that electrons occupy only certain fixed orbits or energy levels.
2. Rutherford’s model did not assign fixed energies to electron orbits; Bohr’s model assigned a definite energy to each allowed orbit.
3. Rutherford’s model could not explain why revolving electrons do not lose energy and fall into the nucleus; Bohr’s model explained atomic stability through stable orbits.
4. In Rutherford’s model, an accelerating electron should continuously radiate energy; in Bohr’s model, an electron in a permitted orbit does not radiate energy.
5. Rutherford’s model did not explain the line spectra of atoms; Bohr explained them by absorption or emission of energy when electrons jump between energy levels.

items.followUp: What is a saturated solution? Describe how crystals can be obtained from it by cooling.

rubric.why: A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution can normally hold at the same temperature.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for stating that it contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution and 1 for specifying that this comparison is at the same temperature.

rubric.why: A hot saturated solution is prepared because more solute can dissolve at a higher temperature.
rubric.description: Describes how the hot saturated solution is prepared.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for preparing a saturated solution at a high temperature.

rubric.why: Careful cooling without disturbance allows the solution to retain excess dissolved solute and become supersaturated.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the hot saturated solution is cooled slowly and carefully without disturbance.

modelAnswer: A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution can normally hold at the same temperature; it is unstable.
Prepare a saturated solution of the solute at a high temperature.
Cool the hot saturated solution slowly and carefully without disturbing it.
The cooled solution can retain excess dissolved solute and is then supersaturated.
